met.short: Metabolic equivalent: a unit of effort where 1 MET is resting energy use, about 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ of oxygen. Moderate effort is roughly 3 to 5.9 METs; vigorous is 6 or more.

mvpa.short: Activity at 3 METs or more: brisk walking and harder. It makes you breathe harder than at rest; vigorous effort (6 METs or more) makes talking in full sentences hard.

all-cause-mortality.short: Death from any cause. A study that counts all-cause mortality does not ask what the person died of, only whether they died in the follow-up period.

accelerometer.short: A small sensor worn on the hip or wrist that records body movement many times a second, so activity is measured instead of recalled from memory.

sedentary-behaviour.short: Waking time spent sitting or lying with very low energy use, such as desk work, driving or watching TV. It is not the same as doing too little exercise.

cardiorespiratory-fitness.short: How well the heart, lungs and muscles together take up and use oxygen in hard exercise. VO2max is the lab measure; clinics often estimate it in METs from a treadmill test.

vital-sign.short: A simple measure taken at most clinic visits that signals overall health, such as pulse, blood pressure, temperature and breathing rate.

risk-factor.short: A trait or habit linked to a higher chance of a disease, such as smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or type 2 diabetes. A risk factor can predict disease without causing it.

treadmill-test.short: A test where speed and slope rise step by step until the person must stop. Fitness is then estimated from how far they got, which is cheaper than measuring oxygen use.

systolic-blood-pressure.short: The higher number in a blood pressure reading: the pressure in the arteries as the heart beats. It is given in mm Hg, and 120 is a typical healthy value.

hba1c.short: A blood test that shows average blood sugar over about three months, in % of haemoglobin that carries sugar. Lower is better in diabetes; a drop of 0.5 to 1 percentage point matters.

hdl-cholesterol.short: The "good" cholesterol: fat-carrying particles in the blood that take cholesterol back to the liver. Higher levels go with lower heart disease risk.

c-reactive-protein.short: A protein the liver releases when the body is inflamed. A slightly raised level that stays high is used as a marker of chronic, low-grade inflammation.

hippocampus.short: A seahorse-shaped brain region needed to form new memories. It shrinks slowly with age, and a smaller hippocampus goes with poorer memory.

observational-study.short: A study that watches what people do and what happens to them, without assigning the behaviour. Cohort studies are observational, so they can show links but struggle to prove cause.

reverse-causation.short: When the supposed outcome causes the supposed exposure: for example, early illness makes people less active, so low activity looks like the cause of early death.

mendelian-randomisation.short: A method that uses gene variants linked to a trait, such as habitual activity, to test cause. Genes are fixed at conception, so illness and lifestyle cannot change them.

healthy-volunteer-bias.short: A bias when people who agree to join a study are healthier than the general population, so absolute risks look too low even if comparisons inside the study stay fair.
